praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A fourth grader with an IEP fluency goal is in a six-week small-group intervention. The special educator needs data next month to keep or change that instruction. Which approach best supports that decision?

options.a: Collect weekly one-minute ORF probes and graph the trend
options.b: Administer one nationally normed reading test at the annual IEP
options.c: Open a full reevaluation this month to recategorize eligibility
options.d: Replace academic probes with an FBA of off-task behavior

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: Instructional decisions during an intervention rest on frequent, comparable curriculum-based measurement, such as weekly oral reading fluency probes graphed against an aimline. A once-a-year achievement test and an eligibility reevaluation answer different questions, and an FBA targets behavior function rather than reading growth.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses annual norm-referenced achievement testing with ongoing progress monitoring used to adjust instruction.
distractorExplanations.c: A comprehensive reevaluation decides continued eligibility; it is too slow and the wrong tool for a six-week instructional tweak.
distractorExplanations.d: An FBA hypothesizes behavior function; it does not measure reading fluency growth toward the IEP goal.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: After a writing unit, a co-teacher needs a quick check of whether students can draft a three-paragraph opinion essay. Which tool is most appropriate for that instructional check?

options.a: An individually administered IQ battery yielding standard scores
options.b: A teacher-designed essay prompt scored with a writing rubric
options.c: A statewide eligibility meeting that uses the IQ composite
options.d: An ABC observation of hallway behavior during passing time

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: A classroom writing prompt scored with a rubric is informal, curriculum-aligned assessment of the skill just taught. IQ batteries and eligibility meetings are formal procedures for classification, not unit checks, and ABC data describe behavior function rather than essay quality.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a formal cognitive battery used in eligibility with informal classroom assessment of a taught writing skill.
distractorExplanations.c: An eligibility meeting classifies special education need; it does not score this week's opinion essays.
distractorExplanations.d: ABC observation is an FBA method; hallway behavior is not a measure of essay composition.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A team just found a student eligible as SLD using WISC and WJ scores. The general educator asks whether those scores should now become the daily reading lesson plans. What is the best reply?

options.a: Use the WISC composite as the weekly reading group placement rule
options.b: Replace all curriculum lessons with the WJ subtest names as units
options.c: Keep eligibility scores for classification and teach from IEP goals
options.d: Remove the student from all general-education reading indefinitely

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: Standardized cognitive and achievement scores help determine eligibility and present levels. Daily instruction is driven by IEP goals, curriculum, and ongoing progress data, not by turning subtests into lesson titles. Eligibility also does not, by itself, remove a student from general-education reading.

distractorExplanations.a: IQ composites are not grouping rules for daily reading; grouping should follow skill needs and IEP goals.
distractorExplanations.b: WJ subtests describe measured skills; they are not a substitute curriculum or unit sequence.
distractorExplanations.d: Eligibility does not automatically equal a more restrictive placement or removal from general-education reading.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A student's disruption spikes when independent math starts and stops when classmates laugh. Before writing a BIP, what should the team collect?

options.a: The student's latest math percentile on a group achievement test
options.b: Adaptive-behavior scores used for intellectual-disability eligibility
options.c: A one-time parent interview with no classroom observation at all
options.d: ABC data across settings to hypothesize the function of disruption

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: A behavior intervention plan should rest on a functional behavioral assessment. Antecedent-behavior-consequence data across settings let the team hypothesize function (here, possibly attention or escape) and match replacement skills. Achievement percentiles, adaptive scores, and a single interview without observation do not identify function.

distractorExplanations.a: A math percentile describes academic standing; it does not identify why disruption occurs when independent work starts.
distractorExplanations.b: Adaptive-behavior scores support ID identification, not the function of classroom disruption.
distractorExplanations.c: Parent input is useful, but an FBA also needs direct ABC observation; interview-only data are incomplete.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: After six weeks of Tier 2 decoding delivered with fidelity, CBM probes show a flat trend well below the aimline. What should the team do next for instruction?

options.a: Keep the same lessons unchanged until the annual state assessment
options.b: Intensify or change the intervention based on the CBM trend
options.c: Exit the student from all reading support as a nonresponder now
options.d: Drop CBM and give a single IQ test to plan next week's lessons

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: Progress monitoring exists to detect nonresponse while there is still time to change instruction. A flat trend below the aimline, with fidelity confirmed, is a signal to intensify or switch the intervention. Waiting for a year-end test, dropping support, or substituting an IQ score for CBM all miss that instructional purpose.

distractorExplanations.a: Annual state testing is too delayed; progress-monitoring rules call for instructional change when growth is inadequate.
distractorExplanations.c: Nonresponse means change the intervention, not abandon reading support.
distractorExplanations.d: IQ scores do not replace frequent CBM when the question is whether this week's decoding instruction is working.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A bilingual student is referred for possible SLD. The psychologist will give a standardized achievement battery. What additional information is most needed so results are not misread as disability?

options.a: Discard classroom work because only standard scores count under IDEA
options.b: Translate the English-normed test on the spot and keep those norms
options.c: Add language-proficiency data and work samples to interpret scores
options.d: Use lunchroom popularity ratings as the primary eligibility measure

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: IDEA requires a variety of assessment tools and nondiscriminatory procedures. Language-proficiency data plus informal classroom work help the team separate limited English or opportunity from a learning disability. Informal data cannot be discarded, on-the-spot translation invalidates norms, and social popularity is not an SLD measure.

distractorExplanations.a: IDEA forbids using a single formal score as the sole criterion; classroom evidence is part of a comprehensive evaluation.
distractorExplanations.b: Ad hoc translation changes the task, so published English norms no longer apply.
distractorExplanations.d: Peer popularity is unrelated to SLD identification and is not a valid eligibility measure.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A special educator wants weekly classwide CBM math probes in a co-taught class to guide grouping. A colleague says parent consent for a special education evaluation is required first. What is accurate?

options.a: Any CBM probe is an initial evaluation and needs signed consent
options.b: Weekly probes replace any later need for an eligibility evaluation
options.c: Progress probes are allowed only after the student is already IDEA-eligible
options.d: Instructional probes are not an initial evaluation needing that consent

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: Classwide instructional assessment, including CBM used to group and pace teaching, is not the IDEA initial evaluation. Informed parental consent is required before that evaluation and before initial services. Probes neither trigger consent by themselves nor replace a later comprehensive evaluation if a student is referred.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses routine classroom progress checks with the formal initial evaluation that requires consent.
distractorExplanations.b: CBM can screen and monitor but cannot substitute for a comprehensive eligibility evaluation.
distractorExplanations.c: General-education progress monitoring is appropriate before eligibility; it is part of RTI/MTSS, not a post-eligibility privilege.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: The team hypothesizes that a student's shouting is maintained by escape from writing tasks. Which BIP element best matches that function?

options.a: Teach a break request and fade writing demand while building stamina
options.b: Increase loud public reprimands so the shouting is punished more visibly
options.c: Add extra writing pages as a consequence each time shouting occurs
options.d: Ignore antecedents and only tally shouting frequency on a clipboard

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: A function-based BIP teaches a replacement that meets the same need with lower cost. If shouting is escape-maintained, a taught break request plus temporarily reduced demand and skill-building addresses the function. Extra writing or public reprimands can worsen escape- or attention-maintained behavior, and frequency counts without antecedents do not implement a plan.

distractorExplanations.b: Public reprimands may supply attention and do not teach an escape-appropriate replacement skill.
distractorExplanations.c: Adding writing increases the aversive demand, which can strengthen escape-maintained shouting.
distractorExplanations.d: Tallying frequency is measurement, not a function-matched intervention.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: September universal screening shows many students below the computation benchmark. After Tier 2 intervention starts, what is the distinct role of progress monitoring?

options.a: Repeat the same universal screener once a year with no instructional change
options.b: Give frequent brief probes to see if the intervention produces growth
options.c: Use one progress-monitoring sitting as the sole IDEA eligibility test
options.d: Give a full cognitive battery to every student below the screening cut

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: Universal screening identifies who is at risk; progress monitoring then uses frequent brief probes to judge whether the chosen intervention is producing adequate growth. It is not a once-a-year screener, not a standalone eligibility test, and not a reason to give every below-cut student an IQ battery.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses annual screening with ongoing progress monitoring that is meant to change instruction in weeks, not a year.
distractorExplanations.c: A single probe cannot serve as the sole eligibility criterion; IDEA requires a comprehensive evaluation.
distractorExplanations.d: Screening cut scores trigger instructional intervention, not automatic cognitive testing of every student.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A teacher notes that a student “looks lost” during science labs and wants to use that observation as the sole basis for an intellectual disability eligibility decision. What is the problem?

options.a: Informal anecdotal notes are illegal to keep in any student education file
options.b: Science labs cannot be observed because they are not academic content
options.c: Eligibility needs a full evaluation, not one informal impression
options.d: Informal observation is sufficient under IDEA for ID eligibility

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: Informal observation is useful instructional and ecological information, but IDEA eligibility for intellectual disability requires a comprehensive evaluation, typically including cognitive and adaptive measures and multiple sources. A single impression cannot classify. Anecdotal notes are not illegal, and science is academic content.

distractorExplanations.a: Classroom notes may be kept; the error is using them as the sole eligibility measure, not that they are forbidden.
distractorExplanations.b: Science labs are academic settings and are appropriate places to observe participation and skill.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the rule: informal observation alone cannot establish ID eligibility under IDEA.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A student's reading comprehension standard score is 82 on a norm-referenced test. The IEP team is writing present levels. How should that score be used?

options.a: Treat it as a grade equivalent proving the student reads at grade 2
options.b: Use it as the only present-level statement with no classroom data
options.c: Treat it as proof the student cannot access general-science content
options.d: Use it with informal classroom and CBM data in present levels

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: A standard score is one formal snapshot against a norm group. Present levels should integrate that score with informal classroom work and progress-monitoring probes. Standard scores are not grade equivalents, cannot stand alone, and do not by themselves bar access to general-education content.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses standard scores with grade equivalents, which are easily misread and do not prove a uniform grade-2 skill set.
distractorExplanations.b: Present levels need multiple sources; a single formal score omits instructional performance.
distractorExplanations.c: A comprehension score does not automatically deny science access; instruction and accommodations address access.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A para records that a student left the seat 14 times in 30 minutes but does not note what happened before or after. Why is this insufficient for an FBA?

options.a: Frequency without antecedents and consequences cannot identify function
options.b: Fourteen instances is too high a number to count in special education
options.c: Seat-leaving can be assessed only with a processing-speed IQ subtest
options.d: FBAs require a statewide standardized behavior percentile and nothing else

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: An FBA seeks the function of behavior. Rate or frequency is useful, but without antecedents and consequences the team cannot tell whether leaving the seat is escape, attention, access, or sensory. There is no magic count threshold, IQ subtest, or statewide percentile that replaces ABC analysis.

distractorExplanations.b: High frequency is a reason to assess, not a reason that counting is invalid; the missing piece is context.
distractorExplanations.c: Processing-speed scores belong to a psychoeducational battery, not an FBA of seat-leaving.
distractorExplanations.d: FBAs are based on interviews and ABC observation; they are not a single statewide behavior percentile.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: At a progress-report period, a student with SLD is meeting CBM aimlines on IEP reading goals. The assistant principal asks if the team should dismiss eligibility today based on those probes alone. Best response?

options.a: Yes — one strong CBM series automatically ends IDEA eligibility today
options.b: No — CBM informs IEP goals; dismissal requires a reevaluation decision
options.c: Yes — meeting goals means the original eligibility evaluation was invalid
options.d: No — students with SLD can never have IEP goals revised when they grow

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: Progress monitoring shows whether instruction is closing IEP goals; it does not by itself end eligibility. Exiting special education is a team decision after a reevaluation (or parent agreement to waive) and notice. Meeting goals is a success of instruction, not proof the original evaluation was wrong, and goals can be revised as the student grows.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses instructional progress with the separate eligibility/exit decision, which needs a reevaluation process.
distractorExplanations.c: Growth toward goals is the point of special education; it does not retroactively invalidate eligibility.
distractorExplanations.d: IEP goals should be updated when the student masters them; SLD does not freeze goals forever.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A student on alternate academic achievement standards needs evidence of growth toward IEP skill goals between formal testing windows. Which classroom evidence best documents that growth?

options.a: A single national percentile unused for any classroom instructional planning
options.b: Deleting work samples so only the psychologist's report remains on file
options.c: Dated work samples and task-analytic probes across the marking period
options.d: A one-day IQ retest each Friday in place of any teacher-collected data

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: Between formal alternate-assessment windows, informal and curriculum-based evidence—dated work samples, task analyses, and frequent probes—shows skill growth and guides instruction. A unused national percentile, discarding work, or weekly IQ retests do not document IEP skill progress in the classroom.

distractorExplanations.a: A unused norm-referenced percentile is a formal snapshot, not ongoing evidence of IEP skill growth.
distractorExplanations.b: Work samples are core informal evidence; deleting them leaves the team without instructional documentation.
distractorExplanations.d: Weekly IQ retesting is not progress monitoring of IEP skills and is the wrong formal tool for weekly instruction.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A behavior specialist completes an FBA showing attention-maintained calling out. The principal asks whether the FBA now places the student under the emotional disturbance category. Accurate reply?

options.a: Yes — completing an FBA is itself an IDEA eligibility determination
options.b: Yes — calling out is sufficient by itself for an emotional-disturbance label
options.c: No — FBA data cannot be shared with the IEP team under any circumstances
options.d: No — FBA informs the BIP; categorical eligibility is a separate decision

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: An FBA is an assessment of behavior function used to design a BIP and support instruction. Disability category (including ED) is a multidisciplinary eligibility decision using IDEA criteria and multiple sources. Completing an FBA neither labels the student nor hides the data from the IEP team.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a functional assessment of behavior with the separate IDEA eligibility determination.
distractorExplanations.b: Calling out, even if attention-maintained, does not meet ED criteria by itself.
distractorExplanations.c: FBA results should be shared with the IEP team so the BIP and supports can be written; they are not confidential from the team.
